claims.claim: Free will is a contested concept often characterized minimally as a person's capacity to choose and control actions, while philosophers disagree about its exact nature and even whether it exists.

Freedom of action and free will are closely related but distinguishable: an external obstacle can prevent someone from carrying out a choice, while questions about free will also concern the relevant kind of control in choosing and acting.
Compatibilism is the thesis that free will is compatible with causal determinism, whereas incompatibilism denies that they can both obtain.
Incompatibilist arguments may focus on whether an agent could have done otherwise or whether the agent is the appropriate source of the action; these are different proposed conditions for freedom.
Compatibilist accounts commonly distinguish ordinary causal influence from coercion or manipulation and may emphasize an agent's reasons-responsive or evaluative capacities.
Indeterminism or randomness alone does not settle the free-will problem, because a theory must still explain how the agent has the relevant kind of control over the action.
Free will is often connected to moral responsibility, but philosophers dispute both the nature of that connection and whether the same control is required for each.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether causal determinism rules out free will.
positions: Compatibilists hold that free will can coexist with causal determinism, often by analyzing freedom in terms of an agent's reasons, capacities, or lack of constraint.
Incompatibilists hold that causal determinism and free will cannot both obtain, often citing alternative possibilities or sourcehood.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the disagreement as a dispute over conditions for freedom and does not treat either position as established.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the ability to do otherwise is necessary for free will or moral responsibility.
positions: Alternative-possibilities accounts treat genuine alternatives as central to freedom.
Some compatibilist and sourcehood-oriented accounts reject or qualify that requirement.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson identifies alternative possibilities as one candidate condition and distinguishes it from sourcehood rather than deciding the controversy.
